#divinemercy  #catholicchurch #catholicprayer #jesus 

Why Some Souls Need Purgatory — The Catholic Teaching Many People Overlook || Fulton J. Sheen

What happens to the soul that dies in God’s grace but is not yet fully purified? The Catholic teaching on Purgatory reveals a profound truth about sin, holiness, divine mercy, and the soul’s preparation for Heaven. Yet this important teaching is often misunderstood or overlooked.

In this powerful reflection inspired by Catholic teachings and the spiritual wisdom associated with Fulton J. Sheen, discover why Purgatory matters, how God’s mercy and justice work together, and why prayer for the Holy Souls remains an important Catholic devotion. Explore what Scripture and the Catholic Church teach about purification after death—and how this belief can transform the way you live, pray, and prepare your soul for eternity.

WHAT YOU WILL DISCOVER:
- Why some souls undergo purification before entering Heaven
- The Catholic understanding of Purgatory and divine mercy
- The connection between sin, holiness, and eternal life
- Why Catholics pray for the Holy Souls in Purgatory
- How prayer, repentance, and confession shape your spiritual life
- What this teaching reminds us about death, judgment, and eternity

Purgatory is not a rejection of God’s mercy; in Catholic teaching, it reflects His work of purification in those who die in His grace. Let this message inspire you to seek holiness, receive God’s mercy, and remember the souls who depend on the prayers of the faithful.

Watch until the end, reflect on these timeless teachings, and share this message with someone who wants to understand the Catholic faith more deeply.

Subscribe to THE HIDDEN GOSPEL for more Catholic teachings, biblical reflections, prayers, and spiritual wisdom that help you grow closer to Jesus Christ.

transcript.text: You wonder, perhaps, why a soul that has been washed in the blood of the Lamb should still need cleansing.
You wonder why a God who is love itself would allow any suffering to remain for those he has already claimed as his own.

And perhaps beneath that wonder, there is a quieter fear—a fear you have never spoken aloud—that the doctrine of purgatory is simply too hard, too severe, too much like a second hell created by a God who cannot quite bring himself to forgive completely.
Look into your own heart for a moment.
Think of the last time you received forgiveness for a serious sin.
Perhaps you knelt in the confessional, the priest raised his hand, and the words of absolution fell upon you like cool water on a parched soul.
You walked out of that little room with a heart lighter than it had been in months.
And yet that same evening, you found yourself short-tempered with your family.
You found yourself returning to the very thoughts and habits you had just confessed.
You had been forgiven, truly and completely, and yet something remained.
Something had not yet been healed.
Something had not yet been burned away.
That is where the mystery of purgatory begins to reveal itself, not as a place of divine cruelty, but as the final, necessary work of a love that refuses to leave us half-finished.
My dear soul, listen carefully.
The Church does not teach that purgatory exists because God's mercy is insufficient.

She teaches that purgatory exists precisely because God's mercy is so complete that he will not rest until the last stain, the last attachment, the last shadow of selfishness has been drawn out of the soul and consumed in the fire of his love.
The souls in purgatory are not there because they are unloved.
They are there because they are loved too much to be left as they are.
The Catechism of the Catholic Church puts it with a clarity that should stir both awe and gratitude:

All who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are indeed assured of their eternal salvation, but after death they undergo purification so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven.
Why would a soul that is destined for the eternal joy of heaven need to be cleansed by fire?
Turn with me in your minds to the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 3.
Saint Paul speaks to us there, not of milk for babes, but of the fire that tests the work of every man.
He tells us that no one can lay a foundation other than the one that is there, Jesus Christ.
He speaks of building upon this foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones, or with wood, hay, and straw.

transcript.text: He knows that we are weak.
He knows that many die in a state of grace loving God, but still attached to lesser things.
They die with the debt of temporal punishment unpaid.
They have been forgiven of the eternal guilt of sin through the confessional, yes,
but they have not yet made satisfaction for the temporal consequences of their sins.
Think of a child who breaks a neighbor's window.
The father forgives the child, but the window must still be paid for.
So it is with God.
He forgives the sin, but justice demands that the disorder caused by sin be repaired.
This is the doctrine of purgatory.
It is not a place of punishment for the sake of vengeance, but a place of purification for the sake of love.
It is the goldsmith holding the precious metal in the fire.
The goldsmith does not hold the fire to destroy it, but to remove the dross so that the gold may be pure and reflect the light perfectly.
You are that gold.
God is the goldsmith.
The fire of purgatory is the intense love of God, which burns away everything in you that is not of God, everything that resists his grace, so that you can finally look upon his face without shame.
Now, the thought of this purification might fill you with fear, but I tell you it should fill you with hope.
For the souls in purgatory are the friends of God.
They are in a state of grace.
They are assured of their salvation.
They cannot sin anymore.
They suffer, yes, but their suffering is not despair.
It is a suffering of longing, of waiting, and of that joyful peace which comes from knowing that they are loved and that their journey is not over, but merely passing through the last gate.
They are like the travelers who have reached the city's walls, but must wait for the gates to be opened.
They are like the bride who is making her final preparations for the bridegroom.
But here is the great mystery that we must embrace.
We, the church militant here on earth, can help them.
We can speed them on their way.
This is the meaning of the doctrine of the communion of saints.
We are not isolated individuals.
We are one body in Christ.
If one member suffers, all suffer together.
If one member is honored, all rejoice together.
When we pray for the dead, when we offer the holy sacrifice of the mass for them, when we offer our alms, our fasting and our penances on their behalf, we are sending relief to the suffering church.
Imagine the souls in purgatory as men and women trapped in a burning building, not a building of destruction, but a building of refining.
They cannot escape on their own, but they can be pulled out by the hands of those who love them.
That hand is your prayer.
That hand is your rosary.
That hand is the Holy Mass.
There is no greater act of charity you can perform for another human being than to pray for the repose of their soul.
You cannot pray for the souls in hell, for their choice is fixed.
But for the souls in purgatory, your prayer is a lifeline.
It is a drop of water on a parched tongue.
It is a light in the darkness.
It is a currency that buys back time.
I remember hearing stories from the missions...
